title: Assigning Animations | Why "Make It Look Cool" Is Not Enough to Get the Movement You Want

scenes.title: Communicating the Intended Movement
lines: The fighter ducks under a high kick, then immediately follows with another attack. Even this brief movement in Virtua Fighter involves body orientation, foot placement, and distance from the opponent. If you ask the person making this animation simply to make it look cool, will you both imagine the same result? Today, we will define the work with an animation list, communicate intent through poses and timing, and explore how a team refines the resulting movement together.

A character's posture at one instant is called a pose. A sequence of those poses over time is animation. Walking boldly with the shoulders back and walking cautiously with the head lowered create very different impressions. An animation brief should describe the action and the feeling it needs to convey.

Here are two walks from Unreal’s Game Animation Sample. The figure on the left walks upright. The one on the right walks with bent knees. Watch the height of the head and the bend at the knees. Here is one way to turn “cautiously” into a usable direction. Keep the head from rising sharply as the feet trade support. The animator can now see exactly what to check.

scenes.title: Animation Lists and Timing
lines: To communicate that intent completely, start with an animation list. List the animations you need, such as standing idle, walking, and attacking, and describe what each one does. For an attack, specify where the body and hands move, how long the action lasts, and when its hit detection becomes active and stops being active.

Hit detection determines whether an attack connects. The entire time the arm is moving and the time it can actually hit an opponent may be different. The example on screen uses timing we have chosen. At sixty frames per second, one second is divided into sixty intervals. If hit detection is active for twelve frames, twelve divided by sixty gives zero point two seconds. Specify this interval separately from the full animation so the visual movement and the required game rules can work together.

That duration is not chosen in isolation. Consider the opponent's time to notice and respond, along with the flow into the next action, when deciding it. Idle and walking animations, meanwhile, need to continue beyond one playback. They need a smooth return from the end to the start: repeated playback, or a loop. Record whether an animation plays once or repeats while its condition remains true in the list as well.

scenes.title: Turning Words into Pose References
lines: We have now defined what happens and when. But the shape the body should make is still described only in words. Even an instruction to extend the right arm forward can look different depending on shoulder height, elbow direction, and the body's lean. There are many possible poses. Showing the pose directly makes those differences much clearer.

One method is to pose an articulated figure and photograph it. Simplify the background and mark the hands and feet to make a reference. Here, we view an Unreal mannequin’s first step from two angles. At the same instant the feet can overlap from one angle, while the other angle reveals which foot is leading. For the reference pose, choose the angle that separates the feet and note which foot should carry the weight and where the body should face. Put that still beside the finished motion to see how much of the original intent comes through.

scenes.title: Comparing the Reference and the Animation
lines: You can place that reference beside the resulting animation for comparison. For a punching pose, matching the hand position is only part of the task. Which foot carries the weight, which way the torso turns, and how the body moves into the next pose should all be readable together. Comparing the motion around a single reference pose helps reveal where the intended feeling starts to change.

When two characters make contact, their relative positions also become a requirement. Super Smash Bros. Ultimate has different characters compete through attacks and movement. Watch Samus grab and lift her opponent, then throw them upward. The grabbing hand and the opponent's body need to move together. Each animation may look natural on its own, yet when the characters are brought together, their positions or timing can be out of step. For these actions, include the other character in the reference.

A weapon adds more things to check. Inkling, from the same game, is a character who uses ink. Watch both the body's direction and the path of the weapon. A drawing that shows only the arm's pose can miss the weapon's size and the space it needs. Show the attack direction and the weapon's trajectory to make the required movement clear.

For a dodge, consider what is being avoided and which way the body moves away. For an idle pose, consider how personality comes through even while the character is standing still. The same applies to greetings and celebratory gestures. Different kinds of movement call for different emphasis in the reference. Rather than attaching the same pose to every scene, preserve the conditions that make each movement recognizable.

scenes.title: Choosing References for the Body
lines: If a character inherits an already familiar movement, that movement itself can serve as the reference. Capture its distinctive gestures at key moments, and explain which poses and rhythms the new animation should retain. In some cases, an existing scene communicates the intent more accurately than a new figure photograph. In this demonstration of one gesture on two characters, keeping the reference pose beside them lets us compare which features to preserve.

A different body structure may call for a different method. In Untitled Goose Game, you control a goose, move objects around, and cause trouble for people. A goose does not pick things up with hands. It lowers its neck to grasp them with its beak, then carries them by moving its neck and body. Rather than forcing this into a human-shaped figure, describe where the beak should move and when it should grasp the object using text and a path. The purpose of reference material is not to fill out a fixed template, but to show exactly what that body needs to do.

scenes.title: From a Document to Movement
lines: Even with all this preparation, the animation is not yet complete. A photograph shows a single instant, while a game shows the continuous movement into and out of that pose. Shifting the body's balance, placing the feet, and connecting to the next movement require decisions that are made while building the actual animation.

Compare the last step in these two stops. One clip uses the left foot as its reference, the other the right. In the final pose both are standing still, so it is easy to miss the difference. Keep the foot position before the stop beside the settled pose. The animator can then tell which leg is meant to receive the weight.

The reference figure and the game character do not have identical bodies, either. How far a joint can move, such as how high an arm can lift, is called its range of motion. A pose that works on the figure may deform the model's shoulder or cause it to intersect a prop. Instead of forcing the model to match the photograph, preserve the intended force and direction through a different solution.

scenes.title: Refining the Result and Sharing What You Learn
lines: That is why reviewing the result involves more than checking it against the first document. Check whether the action reads at its actual speed, whether it retains the character's identity, and whether it feels good when combined with the controls. Some ideas need revision, and others may need to be dropped for a better result. The document gives everyone a shared target, and the moving result lets the team reassess that target.

Finally, watch the change of direction at normal speed. Compare left and right turns from the same camera. You can read how the torso follows the planted foot. When requesting a revision, go beyond “make it more natural.” Specify which footfall should coincide with the change of facing.

The lessons learned from those revisions are worth sharing beyond the person responsible. Explain why a foot position changed, or which pose intersected a weapon, to reduce the same mistakes in other animations. Define the work with an animation list, communicate intent through poses and timing, and refine the resulting movement together. A good animation brief does not demand that someone get it right on the first try. It provides concrete guidance that helps the team reach the intended result together.
